This form ensures compliance with the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act) and the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Regulation 2025. Failure to comply is an offence under the legislation, with a maximum penalty of 20 penalty units.

chunks.heading_path: Rental scams > Check the processes and know your rights
chunks.body:
In Queensland, rental bonds must be lodged with the RTA. If you give your bond to the property manager/owner, make sure you receive a receipt for the amount paid. You should also get a receipt for any other monies paid, such as a holding deposit or rent. Once the property manager/owner receives the bond, they have 10 days to lodge it with the RTA.
You can also lodge your bond yourself using RTA Web Services. This option ensures that any bond money comes directly to the RTA for safekeeping.
No matter how you pay your bond, once it is lodged with the RTA, you will receive a bond acknowledgement from the RTA.

chunks.heading_path: Rental scams > Further information and support
chunks.body:
The cyber.gov.au website includes a guide for how to report and recover from scams.
The RTA investigates alleged offences under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008, and may refer matters to other agencies. This may include the Office of Fair Trading if the scam involves a real estate agent or agency and the Queensland Police Service where investigations uncover evidence of unlawful behaviour outside of the Act – such as fraud and theft.

title: RTA: Rent bidding
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Rent bidding
chunks.body:
A rental property must be advertised at a fixed price - failing to do so is an offence. The property manager/owner does not have to display the price on a ‘for rent’ sign at the property, but any other advertisement must include a fixed price.
A property manager/owner must also not:
- advertise a property with a rent range (e.g. between $420-$460 a week)
- put a property up for rent auction
- proactively tell rental applicants to offer over the advertised rental price and encourage them to outbid each other or accept offers of higher amounts over the advertised rental price.
This is an offence under the Act, with a maximum penalty of 50 penalty units.
You can anonymously report an advertised rental property or room where rent is not at a fixed price via our online form.
From 6 June 2024, a property manager/owner cannot, at the start of a new tenancy, solicit, accept or invite a tenant to pay more rent in advance that exceeds two weeks for a periodic tenancy agreement, rooming accommodation agreement or movable dwelling tenancy agreement and one month for a fixed tenancy agreement, even if a prospective tenant makes an offer to pay more than the amount prescribed in the legislation. This is an offence under the Act, with a maximum penalty of 50 penalty units.
A person is not allowed to accept a rental bond from the tenant if the premises were advertised or offered without a fixed amount of rent. This is also an offence under the Act, with a maximum penalty of 50 penalty units.
Note: throughout the course of a tenancy, a tenant may negotiate how much rent in advance can be paid.
A customer who believes that rent bidding has taken place can contact the RTA for advice and request an investigation.

chunks.heading_path: Rent bidding
chunks.body: More information about rent bidding and how to navigate a tight rental market can be found in our webinar Your questions answered: searching for a rental, rent and ending a tenancy.

chunks.heading_path: Rent bidding > Case study 1
chunks.body:
Scenario: A property has been advertised online with no rental price. Sam wants to apply for the property so rings the agent to ask how much it costs a week to rent. He is told there is no fixed price for the rent and he should put in his best offer. Sam puts in an offer and secures the property.
Analysis: The property manager has acted illegally and encouraged rent bidding by not advertising the property at a fixed price.

chunks.heading_path: Rent bidding > Case study 2
chunks.body:
Scenario: Ali proactively puts in an offer for a rental property, offering to pay two months' rent in advance and an extra $15 a week over the rental asking price. The property manager accepts her offer and she secures the rental property.
Analysis: The property manager has acted illegally. Although the property manager has not encouraged rent bidding, they must not accept the offer to pay over the asking price and two months' rent in advance for the rental property.

chunks.heading_path: Rent bidding > Case study 3
chunks.body:
Scenario: Maria secures a rental property and has been asked to pay one month rent in advance. Three months into her tenancy she receives a lump sum payment from work and offers to pay her next three months rent in advance to help her manage her household budget more effectively. The property manager accepts her three months rent in advance.
Analysis: The property manager has not acted illegally. The property manager only took one month rent in advance upon starting the tenancy agreement. Maria negotiated with the property manager during the tenancy to pay further rent in advance and as the agreement had commenced, this is not illegal.

title: RTA: Student accommodation
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation
chunks.body:
As a student, it may be your first time moving out of home and renting a place to live. The information below is about types of accommodation, support for multicultural students and the 4 main stages of renting – before you rent, starting a tenancy, during and ending a tenancy.
On this page
- Types of student accommodation
- Before you rent
- Multicultural and international students
- Starting a tenancy
- During a tenancy
- Ending a tenancy
- Gender-based violence in student accommodation
- Further information

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Types of student accommodation
chunks.body: Students can live in different types of rental properties. Student accommodation can include:

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Types of student accommodation > On-campus student accommodation
chunks.body:
On-campus student accommodation isn’t covered by the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act), the legislation administered by the RTA.
If you pay a rental bond, it must still be lodged with the RTA. The RTA can help with bond enquiries but may not be able to help with general questions about this type of accommodation.
A lot of the information on this webpage may not apply to you if you live in on-campus student accommodation.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Types of student accommodation > Off-campus privately owned student accommodation
chunks.body:
Privately owned student accommodation is often a type of rooming accommodation. This means you will have your own room, and share other facilities such as kitchens, bathrooms and living areas. Rooming accommodation is different to living in a share house.
You may need to prove you are a student to live in this type of accommodation.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Types of student accommodation > Private rental properties or rooms
chunks.body:
Options include:
- renting a room in an existing share house as part of a co-tenancy or sub-letting
- renting a property with friends as part of a co-tenancy
- renting a property on your own.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Types of student accommodation > Homestay programs
chunks.body: These involve renting a room in a private home, usually with a family in the local area. Meals and other services may be provided as part of the rent. Homestay programs are similar to boarder/lodger arrangements and they aren’t covered under the Act. If you pay a bond, it must be lodged with the RTA.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Before you rent
chunks.body:
- To help you choose a place, use the RTA’s property checklist.
- Look out for rental scams.
- Learn about the rental application process.
- For quick renting tips, follow the RTA on Instagram.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Multicultural and international students
chunks.body: Resources and support are available for multicultural students, including information in other languages and interpreter services.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Multicultural and international students > Contacting the RTA
chunks.body: Information about how to contact the RTA is available in 27 different languages. You can also request an interpreter when you call.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Multicultural and international students > Information in other languages
chunks.body: The RTA’s Pocket guide for tenants – houses and units (Form 17a) answers commonly asked questions about tenancies including repairs, rent payments, lease agreements and rental bonds. It is available in 8 languages other than English at Pocket guide for tenants – other languages.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Multicultural and international students > Interpreter services for property manager/owners
chunks.body: Your property manager/owner can access the Free Interpreting Service (FIS) provided by Translating and Interpreting Service (TIS National) to help discuss your tenancy.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Multicultural and international students > Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students
chunks.body: If you identify as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander, you can access Songlines, the RTA’s dedicated phone service for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customers. Calls are answered by staff trained to provide a culturally appropriate, sensitive and respectful service when answering questions about renting in Queensland.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Starting a tenancy > New tenant checklist
chunks.body: The new tenant checklist is a list of things to consider at the start of your tenancy. If you’re living in rooming accommodation, you may also find the resident checklist for starting a tenancy helpful.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Starting a tenancy > Tenancy agreements
chunks.body:
Once you find a place you like and have been approved by the property manager/owner, you will usually be provided with a tenancy agreement. The agreement could be:
- a general tenancy agreement – for houses, units and townhouses or
- a rooming accommodation agreement – for rooming accommodation, including off-campus student accommodation.
Read the agreement carefully before you sign it or pay any money. Ensure you understand:
- how much the rental bond is
- rent payments – including the amount, how to pay and when to pay
- the date of the last rent increase
- what is included such as furniture, internet or other services
- any service charges or water charges that you are responsible for
- any special terms in the agreement
- whether the agreement is fixed-term (has a specific end date) or periodic (no set end date).
There can be penalties for ending a fixed-term agreement early. If the length of the lease isn’t right for you and your study plans, try to negotiate a change before you sign the agreement.
If you’re signing an agreement with other people as co-tenants, you are jointly responsible for meeting the agreement terms, including paying the rent in full and on time.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Starting a tenancy > Other tenancy documents
chunks.body:
In addition to your tenancy agreement, you must also be given:
- a copy of the house rules for rooming accommodation
- a copy of the by-laws for units/townhouses in a body corporate
- the Pocket guide for tenants – houses and units (Form 17a) if the agreement is a general tenancy agreement
- a receipt for any money paid, such as rent or your bond.
For general tenancy agreements, the property manager/owner must give you a signed copy of the entry condition report for you to complete. For rooming accommodation, if you paid a bond you must also be given a condition report to complete.
A step-by-step guide for completing the report is available on the entry condition report page.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Starting a tenancy > Rental bond
chunks.body:
If you pay a rental bond, it must be lodged with the RTA. You can lodge the bond with the RTA directly or it can be lodged on your behalf by your property manager/owner.
The easiest way to lodge a bond yourself is to use the Online Bond Lodgement Web Service.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > During a tenancy > Responsibilities
chunks.body:
During a tenancy, you have responsibilities to:
- pay rent and other bills, as specified in your tenancy agreement
- keep the place clean
- follow the house rules for rooming accommodation
- follow the body corporate by-laws for units and townhouses
- carry out maintenance specified in your agreement, such as for lawns, gardens and trees
- report any other repair or maintenance issues to your property manager/owner.
You must request permission from the property manager/owner for tenancy or property changes such as:
- getting a pet
- adding fixtures or making structural changes
- changing tenants
- sub-letting the property.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > During a tenancy > Inspections and entry
chunks.body:
There may be routine inspections by the property manager/owner to check the accommodation. The property manager/owner must follow the rules of entry, giving you notice before they enter your home or room.
In rooming accommodation, the property manager/owner does not need to give notice before entering common areas, such as shared kitchens and living rooms.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > During a tenancy > Rent and rent increases
chunks.body:
During the tenancy it’s important to pay your rent on time. There are limits to how late a payment can be before your property manager/owner can ask you to leave due to non-payment of rent.
A property manager/owner can only increase the rent for a property once every 12 months. Your tenancy agreement should include the date of the last rent increase. If you think a proposed rent increase is excessive, you may wish to talk to the property manager/owner to see if it can be negotiated. If not, you may be able to dispute the increase.
Visit the rent increases page for more information.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > During a tenancy > Issues during a tenancy
chunks.body:
There are steps you can take to work through any issues that affect you, the tenancy or the property with your property manager/owner. Examples include:
- if you experience a break-in or property crime
- if your quiet enjoyment of the property is being disrupted
- if you are experiencing domestic and family violence
- if a natural disaster has impacted the property.
If there is an issue between you and your property manager/owner during your tenancy, possible options are:
- talk to your property manager/owner to try to resolve the issue together
- ask for help from the RTA through our free dispute resolution service
- receive or issue a breach notice.
If you believe an offence has taken place you can request an investigation.
The RTA can only help with disagreements between a tenant/resident and a property manager/owner. If you are having problems with other tenants, it’s best to have a conversation and be proactive, calm and respectful when trying to resolve the issue. Read our tips for self-resolution.
If you live in rooming accommodation, you may also find the resident checklist for during and ending a tenancy helpful.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > During a tenancy > Student status change
chunks.body:
If you stop being a student, your entitlement to live in student accommodation may be affected. You should talk to your property manager/owner about your circumstances.
You may be asked to move out with one month’s notice. Alternatively, you can give your property manager/owner one month’s notice using a Notice of intention to leave (Form 13), or Notice of intention to leave (Form R13) for rooming accommodation, and selecting ‘ending of entitlement to student accommodation’ as the reason.
In some circumstances, your property manager/owner may request a copy of your enrolment status or end of study documents as proof.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Ending a tenancy > Extending or ending your agreement
chunks.body:
When you are approaching the end of your tenancy agreement you can:
- talk to your property manager/owner about extending or renewing the tenancy
- give notice to end the tenancy
- receive notice from your property manager/owner ending the tenancy.
A valid reason must be given to end a tenancy agreement and notice periods apply. You may have to pay reletting costs if you end an agreement early.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Ending a tenancy > Moving out
chunks.body: You can use our step-by-step guide on the vacating a property page to help you prepare for moving out. If you live in rooming accommodation, you may also find the resident checklist for during and ending a tenancy helpful.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Ending a tenancy > Requesting your bond refund
chunks.body:
Either you or the property manager/owner can request a bond refund once the tenancy has ended. Bonds are refunded into Australian bank accounts only. International money transfers and cheques will not be issued.
Tip
International students should keep their Australian bank account open until they have received their bond refund payment from the RTA.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Gender-based violence in student accommodation
chunks.body:
The National Higher Education Code to Prevent and Respond to Gender-based Violence (National Code) sets 7 legally enforceable standards that higher education providers must meet to prevent and respond to gender-based violence, including in student accommodation.
Gender-based violence includes but is not limited to sexual violence, domestic and family violence, technology-facilitated abuse, visa abuse, dating violence, and sexual harassment.
The RTA has developed the guidance below to help student accommodation providers meet their requirements under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act) and the National Code while maintaining student safety and wellbeing.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Gender-based violence in student accommodation > Relocation of tenants/residents due to gender-based violence
chunks.body:
Under the National Code, a student accommodation provider may be required to relocate a tenant or resident. While there is nothing explicit in the Act about relocating a tenant or resident, a provider may:
- seek mutual agreement from the tenant/resident to relocate them with a new agreement
- immediately terminate a resident’s rooming accommodation agreement on the grounds of a serious breach if they have put another person in danger.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Gender-based violence in student accommodation > Mandatory gender-based violence training for tenants/residents
chunks.body:
Under the National Code, student accommodation providers must ensure that tenants/residents complete mandatory training on gender-based violence. While there is nothing explicit in the Act about mandatory training for tenants/residents, a provider may:
- implement training as part of an onboarding process for the property
- include a compliant special term in the tenancy agreement requiring a tenant/resident to complete the training, and where a tenant/resident fails to do so, a provider may issue them with a breach notice.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Gender-based violence in student accommodation > Entry to a property due to gender-based violence
chunks.body:
Under the National Code, student accommodation providers may need to enter a room or property without notice if a gender-based violence disclosure has been made.
While the Act does not specifically include gender-based violence as grounds for entry, it does allow providers to enter a room/property with no notice in an emergency. A gender-based violence disclosure would be appropriate grounds for an emergency entry.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Gender-based violence in student accommodation > RTA investigations and the National Code
chunks.body:
Where a student accommodation provider has acted in line with the National Code, the RTA may receive an investigation request if a tenant/resident believes it was an offence under the Act.
The RTA understands that following the National Code helps protect the safety of residents. We will consider this and whether the provider has acted in the public interest when assessing the investigation request.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Gender-based violence in student accommodation > Domestic and family violence
chunks.body:
Domestic and family violence is a type of gender-based violence. If a tenant/resident is experiencing domestic and family violence, the National Code and the domestic and family violence provisions in the Act both apply.
For more information about the domestic and family violence provisions in the Act, see domestic and family violence in a rental property.

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Further information
chunks.body:
For more information contact the Residential Tenancies Authority.
You can find contact details for other support services and Queensland Government departments on our useful links page.
 | Other languages: You can access a free interpreter service by calling the RTA on 1300 366 311 (Monday to Friday, 8.30am to 5:00pm).

chunks.heading_path: Student accommodation > Pocket guide for tenants - houses and units (Form 17a) v19 1May25
chunks.body: The Pocket guide for tenants - house and units (Form 17a) is for tenants who live in houses, flats, units, townhouses and houseboats. It includes information the tenant will need while renting and explains their rights and responsibilities under the law.

title: RTA: Tenancy databases
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases
chunks.body:
Tenancy databases are registers run by privately owned companies. A tenancy database is a record that holds personal information about someone who has lived in a rental property. It can also include information used for past, present, or future rental agreements.
The RTA does not operate or maintain information on tenancy databases.
Property managers/owners can use these registers during an application process to check the prospective tenant's rental history.
If the property manager/owner finds a listing, they must inform prospective tenants in writing:
- which tenancy databases list the tenant
- what that listing is for, and
- how to have the listing amended or removed.
The Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act) provides protection against incorrect and unfair listings while recognising the property manager/owner’s right to take reasonable steps to protect their property.
Breaching laws relating to tenancy databases carries a penalty of up to 50 units per offence for individuals. The current penalty value for an individual can be found in penalty infringement notices. The penalty unit amount is greater for corporations.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases > When can a tenant be listed?
chunks.body:
Tenants can only be listed on a database if all of the following apply:
- they are named on the tenancy agreement
- the tenancy agreement has ended
- there is a valid reason to list the tenant (see details below)
- all reasonable steps have been taken to advise the tenant of the proposed listing (timeframes apply).

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases > What can a tenant be listed for?
chunks.body:
A tenant can only be listed for one or more of the reasons below:
- Amount owing – if the money owed is more than the rental bond, and: the money owed is not paid on time under a conciliation agreement or order from the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) or the tenant has been served with a Notice to remedy breach (Form 11) for rent arrears and has failed to remedy the breach, or after abandonment of the property, unless the dispute is currently subject to a QCAT determination (and there is no current objection by the tenant).
- Objectionable behaviour – where QCAT has terminated the tenancy agreement for that reason.
- Repeated breaches – where QCAT has terminated the tenancy agreement for that reason.
Please note: If no rental bond has been paid a tenant cannot be listed unless the amount owing is more than one week’s rent.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases > Domestic and family violence
chunks.body: A tenant who has experienced domestic and family violence should not be listed if the breach is the result of the actions of a person using violence. The person using violence can be listed on the database.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases > Changing or removing a listing
chunks.body:
A tenancy database company and the person who makes a listing are both responsible for ensuring the quality of personal information on a database.
If a debt has been paid by a defaulting tenant, the listing must be removed from the database.
If a property manager/owner becomes aware that information they have listed is inaccurate, incomplete or ambiguous they must let the database operator know in writing within 7 days how to amend it. The same applies for removing out-of-date information. They must also keep records of these notifications for a year. The database owner must amend or remove the information within 14 days of being notified. All listings must be removed after 3 years.
The tenant or property manager/owner may also complain to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases > Disputing a listing
chunks.body: A tenant can dispute a listing if it is inaccurate, incomplete, ambiguous and out-of-date or does not meet the listing criteria set out in the Act. They must dispute this within 6 months of becoming aware of the listing.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases > Tenancy database companies
chunks.body:
Tenancy database providers are private companies and may charge for providing information.
Database companies include:
- TICA
- National Tenancy Database
- Trading Reference Australia.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy databases > Tenancy databases
chunks.body: Tenancy databases are legitimate tools that give lessors a means of protecting their property investments.

title: RTA: Preparing for a tenancy
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy
chunks.body:
There are a variety of things property managers/owners and prospective tenants/residents should consider before starting a tenancy. These things range from personal circumstances to your responsibilities under the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act), including special terms in rental agreements and minimum housing standards.
Under the Act, all rental properties must meet minimum housing standards, which aim to ensure all Queensland rental properties are safe, secure and functional. It is crucial that all property managers/owners and prospective tenants/residents are familiar with them.

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Property managers/owner considerations
chunks.body:
Before deciding to rent your property to a tenant/resident there are several things to be aware of.
Whether you choose to manage the property yourself or employ a real estate agent to act on your behalf, the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act) applies.
Your rental property must meet minimum housing standards in addition to ensuring:
- the property is clean and in good repair
- locks and security devices are in good working order
- there is a full set of keys for one tenant/resident and entry keys for all other tenants/residents
- there are contact details for emergency repairs in the tenancy agreement
- you decide if you will take a bond from the tenant/resident
- the property is water efficient if you decide to charge for water consumption.

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Property managers/owner considerations > Reporting concerns
chunks.body: Prospective rental properties can be reported using the Report an advertised rental property for repair concerns form if the premises does not appear to meet minimum housing standards. The RTA's Compliance and Enforcement team will review the report and take further action if required.

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Property managers/owner considerations > Special terms
chunks.body:
Consider if it would be beneficial to include any special terms in the tenancy agreement. A special term is an additional condition that applies throughout the tenancy. Any special terms should be discussed and agreed to before the tenancy agreement is signed. It is important to note that special terms cannot be inconsistent with the Act and it is an offence to enter into a contract which tries to avoid provisions of the Act.
If you own an acreage property or a large block, consider whether the tenant/resident will have access to the entire property. Special terms should clearly state what the tenant/resident does and does not have access to. For example, if there are sheds or areas that you need to access during the tenancy, it is easier to include these in special terms as entry laws apply.

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Property managers/owner considerations > Useful information
chunks.body:
You can find information specifically for property managers/owners under forms and resources, including the Managing general tenancies in Queensland guide.
Application Form: Property managers/owners are required to use a standardised tenancy application form for residential tenancies. This form ensures compliance with the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act) and the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Regulation 2025.

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Prospective tenants/resident considerations
chunks.body:
Before choosing to enter into a tenancy agreement you should first view the prospective rental property you would like to apply for. During inspection it is important to determine if the property meets your needs and is suitable for your lifestyle.
Some things you may like to consider include:
- Is the property the right size?
- Is it in the right location for work and social activities?
- Is it suitable for pets or children?
- Can you maintain the property? (e.g. can you look after a pool, or large garden?)
- Does the property have the facilities you need? (e.g. does it have a broadband connection? If not, can it be added and who will pay for these services to be made available?)
- Will you have to pay for water usage?
- In a rural property, will you need to refill the water tank in dry weather?
- Will there be additional costs for occasional garden maintenance? (e.g. disposing of green waste, tree pruning.)
- In a caravan park, will there be extra site costs?
- If there are gas bottles, will they be filled at the start of the tenancy and will a receipt be provided?
- Does the property have the level of security you require? (e.g. screens on windows.)

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Prospective tenants/resident considerations > Reporting concerns
chunks.body: If, during an in-person or online inspection, you believe a property does not meet minimum housing standards, it is important to report this using the Report an advertised rental property for repair concerns form. The RTA’s Compliance and Enforcement team will review the report and take further action if required.

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Prospective tenants/resident considerations > Special terms
chunks.body:
Before signing the tenancy agreement for your chosen property, you should read the prospective General tenancy agreement (Form 18a) thoroughly. It is important to ask questions if you do not understand something within the agreement, such as additional conditions known as special terms.
Special terms should be discussed and agreed on before signing the tenancy agreement, which is a legally binding contract. Special terms, which cannot be inconsistent with the RTRA Act, often relate to garden and pool maintenance, water charges and even what parts of the property you as a tenant do and do not have access to. It is important to note that it is an offence to enter into a contract which tries to avoid provisions of the RTRA Act.

chunks.heading_path: Preparing for a tenancy > Prospective tenants/resident considerations > Useful information
chunks.body: Find out more about choosing a rental property and use the new tenant checklist to help you prepare before and after signing your tenancy agreement.

title: RTA: Tenancy agreements
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy agreements > What is a tenancy agreement?
chunks.body:
A tenancy agreement – also known as a lease – is a legally binding contract between a property manager/owner and a tenant/resident.
It outlines each party’s legal rights and responsibilities throughout the duration of the tenancy, including the standard terms set out in the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 and any additional special terms agreed to by both parties. A tenancy agreement must be:
- documented in writing
- provided by the property manager/owner to the tenant/resident either on, or before, the day the tenant/resident occupies the premises and before any monies are paid
- accompanied by a copy of either the Pocket guide for tenants – houses and units (Form 17a) or Pocket guide for tenants – caravan parks (Form 17b).
It is an offence not to provide the tenant with a written agreement.
Property managers/owners are responsible for covering the cost of preparing the agreement, which must be written in a clear and precise way.
If a tenant/resident is occupying a premises without a written tenancy agreement, they still have legal protections under Queensland’s tenancy laws and can contact the RTA for support.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy agreements > Types of tenancy agreements
chunks.body:
The Act includes provisions for:
- General tenancy agreements Used when renting a house, unit, apartment, townhouse, houseboat, or secondary dwelling.
- Moveable dwelling agreements Used when renting a caravan, moveable dwelling or site.
- Rooming accommodation agreements Used for boarding houses, supported accommodation services, off-campus student accommodation and other rooming style accommodation.
The Act does not apply to:
- contracts of sale or mortgages if the sale of contract is for 28 days or less
- holiday lettings (e.g. short-stay listings on Airbnb)
- rental purchase plan agreements
- temporary refuge accommodation (e.g. a women’s shelter)
- commercial property (e.g. shop leases)
- renting outside of Queensland.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy agreements > What's included in a tenancy agreement
chunks.body:
All tenancy agreements must include:
- the name and address of the property manager/owner and tenant/resident
- the start and end date of the agreement (or state that it is periodic)
- how the tenant should pay rent and how much is to be paid
- the date of the last rent increase
- contact details for nominated repairers
- standard terms outlined under the Act
- any special terms (these should be agreed in advance, e.g. who is responsible for pool maintenance).
The date of the last rent increase must be included in the tenancy agreement. Tenants have the right to request written proof of the last rent increase during the tenancy, and the property manager or owner must provide this information within 14 days. However, these requirements do not apply in the following cases:
- Exempt Lessors: the Act outlines who qualifies as an exempt lessor.
- For properties purchased between 6 June 2023 and 6 June 2025: the requirement to include the date of the last rent increase in the tenancy agreement and to provide evidence of a rent increase upon the tenant’s request does not apply if the new owner or property manager does not have information about the previous rent increase.
- For properties being rented for the first time: the date of the last rent increase is the date the property is first rented.
Note: A property manager/owner is considered to have evidence of the last rent increase if they or their agent (such as a real estate agent, property manager, or lawyer) has this information.
For more information, please visit our Rent increases webpage.

chunks.heading_path: Tenancy agreements > Rent payment methods
chunks.body:
Property managers/owners must offer tenants/residents at least two options to pay rent. One of these options must not exceed reasonable transactional costs (costs in addition to standard bank transaction fees), and it must be reasonably accessible to the tenant/resident.
Before signing a tenancy agreement, property managers/owners must provide a written notice outlining any associated costs incurred by using the payment methods offered. This is because property managers/owners should be aware of costs associated with the offered payment methods, especially if these costs are not reasonably known by the tenant/resident.
Additionally, property managers/owners must disclose any financial benefits they may receive if the tenant/resident uses a specific rent payment method. For example, if a property manager/owner receives an incentive payment from a third-party platform or a share of the fees charged by the platform, it must be disclosed to the tenant/resident upfront.

title: RTA: Body corporate rental properties
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties
chunks.body:
If you rent, own, or manage a unit, townhouse or apartment, there may be additional body corporate rules that apply as part of community living.
In Queensland, the RTA administers residential tenancy laws and the Office of the Commissioner for Body Corporate and Community Management (BCCM) provides information and assistance on body corporate legislation. This includes the rules on what owners, managers and tenants need to know and comply with.

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > What is a body corporate?
chunks.body:
A body corporate is a legal entity which is created when land is subdivided and registered under the Land Title Act 1994 to establish a community titles scheme. All owners in a community titles scheme are automatically members of the body corporate when they buy their lot.
You can read more about the role of a body corporate on the BCCM website.

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > By-laws and tenancy agreements
chunks.body:
Most complexes of units, townhouses or apartments will have their own set of body corporate by-laws or rules.
The by-laws outline the rules and regulations regarding the use and enjoyment of the lots and common property in the complex. They can cover things such as noise, smoking, pets, parking and the appearance of lots. You can read more about by-laws on the BCCM website.
Under Queensland tenancy laws, the property manager/owner must provide a copy of the relevant by-laws to the tenant when they share the proposed tenancy agreement, as they form part of the tenancy agreement. Failing to do so is an offence.
Tenants should take the time to read and understand the by-laws to ensure they are aware of any restrictions or additional requirements that apply throughout their tenancy.
A breach of a body corporate by-law is a breach of the tenancy agreement, and a Notice to remedy breach can be issued to rectify the issue. The body corporate may also act by issuing a Contravention notice. You can find out more about Contravention notices on the BCCM website.

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > Repairs
chunks.body:
Tenants should contact their property manager/owner regarding any repairs. The property manager/owner will then liaise with the body corporate if required.
Most repairs inside the unit or townhouse will fall to the property manager/owner to rectify (such as a leaking tap), while repairs for the external parts of the property may fall to the body corporate to rectify (such as a leaking roof). Even for repairs that fall to the property manager/owner, there may still be a requirement to notify the body corporate as part of the process.
- RTA website – maintenance and repairs
- BCCM website – maintenance in a body corporate

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > Attaching fixtures and structural changes
chunks.body:
Fixtures are generally items permanently attached to land or a building that are intended to become part of the land or building. Attaching a fixture may include picture hooks, locks, clotheslines, cable TV connections, window awnings, air conditioners, electric vehicle chargers, above ground pools and fencing, carpets, TV antennas, satellite dishes and ramps.
Structural changes are permanent changes to the premises which may include moving or removing walls, changing a window or altering the floor plan.
If a tenant lives in a property managed by a body corporate, and the body corporate's rules or by-laws require approval for adding fixtures or making structural changes, the tenant must complete the Request for Approval to Attach Fixtures or Make Structural Changes (Form 23) and submit it to the property manager or owner. The property manager or owner is required to respond within 28 days, informing the tenant of their decision and stating that approval is subject to the body corporate’s approval. If the property manager or owner approves, they must submit the tenant’s request to the body corporate within 28 days. The body corporate will then review the request, and while there is no set deadline for this review, the property manager or owner must inform the tenant of the body corporate's decision as soon as reasonably possible. If both the property manager or owner and the body corporate approve, the tenant can proceed with the changes according to the agreed conditions.
- RTA website – fixtures and structural changes
- BCCM website – maintenance in a body corporate

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > Minimum housing standards in a body corporate
chunks.body: If a rental property is in a body corporate, it must comply with both minimum housing standards and any body corporate by-laws. There may be instances where the lessor will need to liaise with body corporate to ensure a property complies with minimum housing standards.

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > Pets
chunks.body:
Tenants who rent a property in a body corporate are subject to any by-laws around keeping pets (excluding working dogs). Bodies corporate are not allowed to make by-laws banning pets in community title schemes. However, tenants may need to obtain body corporate committee approval to keep a pet, in addition to approval from the property manager/owner.
- RTA factsheet – renting with pets
- BCCM website – animal by-laws

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > Smoking
chunks.body: Body corporate by-laws may include specification regarding where smoking cigarettes and the use of vape devices can occur at a property, including common areas or balconies. You can find out more about by-laws and smoking on the making by-laws page on the BCCM website.

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > Disputes
chunks.body:
If you have a dispute with either a tenant, a property manager/owner, the body corporate, the committee or another owner or occupier, you are encouraged to try to resolve it with the other party first, before taking any other dispute resolution steps.
Depending on the nature of the dispute, you can access dispute resolution services via:
- RTA dispute resolution – for general tenancy disputes between a tenant and property manager/ owner
- BCCM dispute resolution – for disputes related to body corporate by-laws, body corporate committees or other body corporate specific issues

chunks.heading_path: Body corporate rental properties > Disputes > Further information and support
chunks.body:
Tenants and property managers/owners for body corporate properties can access information and support from the RTA. The RTA resources below provide specific information about body corporate properties:
- Talking tenancies podcast – high density unit living
- BCCM webinar for property managers/owners – part 1
- BCCM webinar for property managers/owners – part 2
BCCM also provide a free information service for those who live, work or invest in Queensland body corporate properties. You can find out more and access resources on the BCCM website.

title: RTA: Retirement villages
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages
chunks.body:
Retirement villages are where senior members of the community or retired persons can choose to live and are generally made up of units or apartments. In some villages, personal care and support services can be bought for a fee.
Residents in retirement villages will often have a residence contract for their accommodation under the Retirement Villages Act 1999. Residence contracts will include things like an upfront cost for the right to reside in the retirement village, ongoing service charges, and exit fees and entitlements. These contracts are different to a rental agreement, and they aren’t covered by the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the RTRA Act). However, there are some circumstances where the RTRA Act applies to a tenancy in a retirement village.
Retirement village providers will also sometimes change a facility’s operations to standard rental accommodation, which is covered by the RTRA Act.
The RTA is only able to provide information and support to providers/managers and tenant/residents if the RTRA Act applies to their tenancy.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > Residence contracts in retirement villages
chunks.body:
A residence contract for accommodation in a registered retirement village is covered by the Retirement Villages Act 1999.
If a resident with a residence contract vacates their accommodation or dies, a relative who has been living with them may be entitled to temporarily stay in the accommodation. This arrangement would also be covered by the Retirement Villages Act 1999, see section 70B for further details and criteria.
Further information about residence contracts is available from the Queensland Government.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > Tenancies covered by the RTRA Act
chunks.body:
If you rent accommodation in a retirement village and don’t have a residence contract, then your tenancy may be covered by the RTRA Act. This includes if you are working at a retirement village and rent accommodation in the facility as part of your employment arrangement.
Depending on the nature of your accommodation, you may have one of the following tenancy agreements: a general tenancy agreement or a rooming accommodation agreement. If a tenancy is covered by the RTRA Act, providers/managers and tenants/residents can contact the RTA for information and support.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > When a retirement village changes operations
chunks.body:
A retirement village provider/manager will sometimes change the purpose and operations of a facility. This could involve changing a facility from a retirement village to standard rental accommodation, such as a seniors’ rental community. The lease arrangements available at a facility may be affected by this.
The provider may also cease to offer personal care and support services at a facility or change the way these services are delivered.
In some cases, the current residents with a residence contract for their accommodation may be given the option to switch to a general tenancy agreement or rooming accommodation agreement. This agreement would be covered by the RTRA Act. New residents may also be offered a general tenancy agreement or rooming accommodation agreement rather than a residence contract.
For support and information about changes to retirement villages, residents should refer to the Queensland Government’s information about retirement villages or contact the Queensland Retirement Village and Park Advice Service (QRVPAS) for free legal help and information.
Providers/managers and tenant/residents can contact the RTA for information and support about new or existing tenancy agreements that fall under the RTRA Act.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > Checking your agreement type
chunks.body:
In some retirement villages, particularly those that are changing to another accommodation type, there may be a mix of residence contracts covered by the Retirement Villages Act 1999 and tenancies covered by the RTRA Act. It’s important to check your agreement to see which Act applies.
Go to tenancy agreements for information about tenancies covered under the RTRA Act.
If you’re unsure if the RTRA Act applies to your agreement, you can ask the provider/manager about the agreement type or contact the RTA for information. You can also make an urgent application to the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) for an order stating if the RTRA Act applies.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > Checking your agreement type > Ending an agreement
chunks.body:
Information is available from the Queensland Government about leaving a retirement village if you have a residential contract you would like to end.
Go to ending a tenancy for information about ending an agreement covered under the RTRA Act.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > Acting on behalf of a resident
chunks.body:
If a tenant/resident would like you to act on their behalf and they have an agreement covered by the RTRA Act, you can either:
- provide a copy of a Power of Attorney to the RTA, or
- ask the tenant/resident to complete a Letter of Authority.
Once the appropriate document is received by the RTA, you will be able to speak to the RTA on behalf of the tenant/resident.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > Acting on behalf of a resident > Further information and support > Residence contracts in retirement villages
chunks.body: Refer to the Queensland Government website for retirement village information. The website also includes a list of useful contacts for getting help in retirement villages.

chunks.heading_path: Retirement villages > Acting on behalf of a resident > Further information and support > Tenancy agreements covered by the RTRA Act
chunks.body: Providers/managers and tenant/residents can contact the RTA for information and support.

title: RTA: Residential services accommodation
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation
chunks.body:
Residential services accommodation is when a resident rents a room or unit that may include services such as meals or personal care. In Queensland, residential services accommodation is usually rented as rooming accommodation.
This page provides information for residents in residential services accommodation and anyone who is supporting them. Residential service providers may also find the information useful. Providers and residents in residential services accommodation sometimes refer to it as supported accommodation.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Residential services accommodation easy read guide
chunks.body: This is an easy read summary of the RTA’s residential services accommodation webpage. It includes information about your agreement, rent, services and how to get help.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Key points to know for residents
chunks.body:
- You should only pay for services you get.
- You can ask for changes to meet your needs.
- If a service stops or is reduced, you can ask to pay less or get money back.
- Free help is available from the RTA and other support organisations.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Information for people supporting residents > Who is a support person
chunks.body:
Residents may have a nominated support person such as a friend, family member, guardian, NDIS support coordinator or support worker. This may be an informal arrangement or a formal arrangement, such as power of attorney. The support person could be someone from an organisation outside of the residential service.
Residents can nominate a support person in their Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18) to receive any forms or notices related to the accommodation.
The staff working in residential services accommodation may also help residents to understand any forms or notices they receive.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Information for people supporting residents > Tips for support people to help residents with their tenancy
chunks.body:
If you are supporting a resident with their tenancy, it can help to:
- read information together
- break information into short sections
- ask the resident to tell you in their own words what each part means
- talk to the RTA or the provider on their behalf
- help the resident write short messages or fill in forms
- keep copies of letters, emails and forms.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Services
chunks.body: Services are things you pay for as part of your rent and must be included in your Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18). If you pay for a service, it must be provided.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Services > Examples of services
chunks.body:
Examples of services include:
- support or supervision
- cleaning, meals or laundry
- security or reception
- management services.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Services > The different levels of services available
chunks.body:
There are three levels of residential services:
- Level 1 – provide accommodation only
- Level 2 – provide accommodation and a food service
- Level 3 – provide accommodation, a food service and personal care (for example: bathing, toileting, dressing, mobility, eating meals, or more).
You can learn more on the Queensland Government residential services page.
This page is primarily for residents in Level 2 and Level 3 residential services accommodation, but residents in Level 1 accommodation may also find it useful.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18)
chunks.body:
You or your nominated representative (for example, family member or support person) will need to read and sign a Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18).
The agreement will tell you:
- how much rent to pay and when
- how long you can stay
- the house rules for the room and accommodation
- what is included, such as meals or other services.
There are penalties if your provider fails to provide a written agreement.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18) > NDIS funded services should not be included
chunks.body:
If you have National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) funding for personal care, your rent should not go toward services that are paid for using this money. Check your agreement doesn’t include anything you pay for with NDIS funding.
For more information about what you can use your NDIS funding for, see supports funded by the NDIS.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18) > If you don't understand the agreement
chunks.body: If you don’t understand the agreement, you should get a support person to help you. You can also contact a support service to help you understand the agreement, such as the ones listed in our Who to contact for help section below.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18) > Your contact for letters and forms
chunks.body:
In your agreement, you can choose someone to get any letters or forms about your accommodation. This could be a family member or other support person. You will still get any letters or forms, but your provider must also give them to your named support person.
If you need help understanding letters or forms about your accommodation, talk to your provider or a friend, family member or support person.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Changes to your services and rent > When a service stops, pauses or changes
chunks.body:
You can ask to pay less rent if a service:
- is no longer available – for example, if a laundry service stops
- is no longer wanted – for example, if you do not need help to bathe anymore, if the meals are not right for you, or if your NDIS plan changes and now pays for some services that were included in your rent
- is reduced – for example, if you get fewer meals each day
- is not needed because you are away – for example, when you are on holiday.
If you’re going away and you pay for a food service that you won’t be using, you can only ask to pay less rent if you are away for more than 2 weeks.
If you get a new service, then your rent may be increased to pay for it.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Changes to your services and rent > Agreeing to changes to services
chunks.body:
Any changes to your services should be agreed between you and your provider. A provider should consider your request fairly.
You can update your rooming accommodation agreement with the changes or put them in writing. You and the provider should agree to the changes.
If you and your provider agree to reduce your rent following a service change, this needs to be in writing. For more information, see rent decreases.
If a service has stopped and you didn’t agree to this or receive a transition plan, talk to your provider. If the service is still available, you can ask for it to start again. You may be able to get some money back if the service stopped while you were still paying for it.
See our Who to contact for help section below for more organisations that may be able to help you if your services change.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Changes to your services and rent > If you go into hospital
chunks.body:
If you go into hospital, you can ask to pay less rent for any personal care services you don’t need because you are away from the accommodation. If you are away for more than 2 weeks, you can also ask to pay less rent for any food services you don’t use while you are away.
You will still need to pay rent to cover your room and accommodation while you are in hospital, but you can ask your provider for a rent decrease.
Any agreement to decrease the rent should be in writing and agreed to by you and your provider. For more information, see rent decreases.
You may want to end or extend your agreement due to a hospital stay or you may be in hospital around the tenancy end date. In either case, you and your provider must follow the correct processes for extending or ending the tenancy.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Changes to your services and rent > Other rent changes
chunks.body:
If your rent is based on how much money you have, it might go up or down with any changes to your income. Only providers who receive government funding through specific programs are allowed to adjust your rent based on your income.
If your rent is not based on your income, your provider will only be able to increase your rent every 12 months. Some providers do not have to follow this rule. For more information, see rent increases.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident
chunks.body: In addition to the rights below, a full list of rights and responsibilities is available in the rights and responsibilities of residents and providers fact sheet.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident > Fair treatment and human rights
chunks.body: You have the right to be treated fairly and for your human rights to be protected. For more information about human rights, see the Queensland Government’s human rights webpage.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident > Residents with disability
chunks.body:
If you have disability, there are laws to protect you from discrimination including the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 and the Anti-Discrimination Act 1991.
To help you choose housing that meets your needs, the Queensland Disability Network has created the My Housing Options toolkit.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident > Services and payments
chunks.body:
You have the right to:
- get all services included in your Rooming accommodation agreement (Form R18)
- not pay for services you aren’t given
- ask what you are paying for
- ask for changes to your agreement if your needs change.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident > Domestic and family violence (DFV)
chunks.body: If you are experiencing domestic and family violence which impacts your accommodation, see the RTA’s domestic violence in a rental property page or contact the RTA for options.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident > Entry and privacy
chunks.body:
Your provider/manager needs to respect your privacy and follow the rules for entry. If your provider/manager wants to inspect your room, they need to give advance notice in writing using an Entry notice (Form R9).
You and your provider/manager may have other agreements about entering your room – for example, to provide services such as personal care or cleaning.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident > Fixtures and structural changes
chunks.body: If you want to add fixtures or make changes to your room or unit (for example, accessibility upgrades), you must get permission from the provider first.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Your rights as a resident > Community visitors
chunks.body: If you have a cognitive impairment or find it hard to make decisions, you may be able to ask a community visitor to check on you and your accommodation. For more information, see the Office of the Public Guardian’s community visitor webpage.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Provider rights and responsibilities
chunks.body: A full list of rights and responsibilities is available in the rights and responsibilities of residents and providers fact sheet.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem
chunks.body: If a resident or a provider breaks a rule in the agreement, there are steps that can be taken.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Talk with each other
chunks.body: Talk to your provider or write to them about what is wrong and what you want to happen. You can also get a support person, such as a friend or family member, to talk to them for you. Keep copies of any letters or messages. For more tips, see self-resolving tenancy issues.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Give a notice asking for a problem to be fixed
chunks.body:
If a problem with your room or accommodation is not fixed, you can use a Notice to remedy breach – rooming accommodation (Form R11). In the notice you can ask the provider to fix the problem within 7 days.
Your provider can also issue you with a notice to fix a problem.
For more information, see breach of the agreement.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Get free help from the RTA with your dispute
chunks.body:
If you and the provider cannot agree about a problem with your room or accommodation, you can request the RTA’s free dispute resolution service. The RTA is neutral and can help you and your provider talk about your problem and come to an agreement.
The RTA cannot help with NDIS funding disputes.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Give notice to leave
chunks.body:
If the problem with your room or accommodation is not fixed within 7 days after you have issued a breach notice, you can give your provider a Notice of intention to leave – rooming accommodation (Form R13).
There are rules about how often someone can enter the room after a Form R13 is given. For more information, see entry to the property.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Being asked to leave
chunks.body:
If your provider has given you a breach notice and you don’t fix the problem within the required timeframe, they may ask you to leave with a Notice to leave – rooming accommodation (Form R12).
If you feel your provider has given you a notice to leave to punish you for asserting your rights, you can dispute the notice. For more information, see retaliatory action.
There are rules about how often someone can enter the room after a Form R12 is given. For more information, see entry to the property.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Apply for a tribunal decision
chunks.body:
You can apply to the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) for a decision about a problem with your room or accommodation. QCAT can order:
- lower rent
- money back
- changes to services
- the agreement to end if needed.
For some problems, you and your provider need to use the RTA’s dispute resolution service before QCAT can help.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Request an investigation from the RTA
chunks.body: The RTA investigates alleged offences under Queensland rental laws. Learn what the RTA can investigate and how to request an investigation.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Complaints about service standards
chunks.body:
You have the right to live in safe, clean and well-managed accommodation. If you think your accommodation and services don’t meet the right standards, you can complain to your provider.
If the problem isn’t resolved, you can complain to the Queensland Government’s Regulatory Services team.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Registration concerns for residential services accommodation
chunks.body:
All residential services accommodation should be registered with the Queensland Government. You can check if a provider is registered by searching for them in the public register of residential services.
If you suspect an unregistered residential service is operating, you can report it to the Queensland Government’s Regulatory Services team.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > NDIS complaints
chunks.body: If you have a problem with the quality or safety of a service funded by the NDIS, you can follow the steps to complain on the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission complaints webpage.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > What to do if there is a problem > Complaints about other residents
chunks.body: If you have an issue with another resident in your accommodation, you can talk to your provider and the resident to see if you can solve the problem together. If the problem can’t be solved, other options are available. For more information, see our quiet enjoyment page.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Who to contact for help > How the RTA can help you
chunks.body:
The RTA can help:
- explain your rental rights and responsibilities
- answer questions about rent, services and your agreement
- resolve rental and bond disputes.
The RTA cannot help with NDIS funding disputes or questions.
You can call the RTA on 1300 366 311 or contact us in a way that works for you.
You can also ask a support person (for example, a friend, family member or support worker) to speak to the RTA on your behalf. If you want to set up a more formal arrangement with the RTA, you can follow the steps for a Letter of Authority and Power of Attorney.

chunks.heading_path: Residential services accommodation > Who to contact for help > Other places that can help
chunks.body:
- QSTARS (Tenants Queensland) – free tenant advice and advocacy services: 1300 744 263.
- Regulatory Services (Department of Housing and Public Works) – registration and complaints about residential services: (07) 3013 2666
- Emergency and temporary housing (Department of Housing and Public Works) – for support in a crisis or if you’re at risk of being homeless. For phone support, call the Homeless Hotline: 1800 474 753
- Supported Accommodation Providers Association Qld (SAPA) – industry information and good practice.
- Office of the Public Guardian – assistance for adults who have difficulty making their own decisions, including a community visitors program: 1300 653 187
- Public Trustee of Queensland – financial administration for adults with impaired decision-making abilities: 1300 360 044
- QCAT – decisions about tenancy disputes and guardianship for adults with impaired decision-making abilities: 1300 753 228
- NDIS – information about NDIS funding including how to apply, eligibility and what it can be used to pay for: 1800 800 110
- Disability Advocacy Pathways – connects Queenslanders with disability, their family, friends and carers with advocacy services to suit their needs and location: 1800 130 582

title: RTA: Secondary dwellings
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Secondary dwellings
chunks.body:
Property owners can choose to rent out secondary dwellings, such as granny flats, to non-household members.
The property owner must obtain all relevant approvals before renting the secondary dwelling, including development/building and council approvals. Owners must also ensure the rental complies with smoke alarm requirements and all other health and safety regulations.
Property managers/owners must require prospective tenants to apply for a residential tenancy agreement using the approved form that complies with the Act. The standardised tenancy application form is the RTA’s Rental Application Form (Form 22). The application form must not request any information beyond what is specified in the RTA’s Application Form (Form 22). Rules apply to the collection, storage, and destruction of personal information gathered during the application process.
For more information visit our application process page.

chunks.heading_path: Secondary dwellings > Types of tenancy agreements for secondary dwellings
chunks.body:
Depending on the set up of the property, a secondary dwelling may be rented out as either a:
- general tenancy agreement, if the secondary dwelling is let out as a self-contained unit and the tenant/resident has no access to the main house
- rooming accommodation agreement, if the tenant/resident shares the kitchen or other facilities with other occupants of the house.
Examples of a secondary dwelling falling under a rooming accommodation agreement could be:

chunks.heading_path: Secondary dwellings > Scenario 1
chunks.body: A rental where a granny flat contains more than one bedroom and each bedroom has been let out separately, with the residents sharing the facilities contained within the flat.

chunks.heading_path: Secondary dwellings > Scenario 2
chunks.body: A rental where the granny flat does not have a kitchen and the occupier is permitted to access the main house to use the kitchen or other facilities.

chunks.heading_path: Secondary dwellings > Scenario 2 > The agreement must include:
chunks.body:
- the address of the main property
- what building (or part of the building) is being rented
- how utilities (including gas and electricity) and water must be paid
- any special terms (see below).
Property managers/owners must offer tenants/residents at least two options to pay rent. One of these options must not exceed reasonable transactional costs (costs in addition to standard bank transaction fees), and it must be reasonably accessible to the tenant/resident.
Before signing a tenancy agreement, property managers/owners must provide a written notice outlining any associated costs incurred by using the payment methods offered. This is because property managers/owners should be aware of costs associated with the offered payment methods, especially if these costs are not reasonably known by the tenant/resident.
Additionally, property managers/owners must disclose any financial benefits they may receive if the tenant/resident uses a specific rent payment method. For example, if a property manager/owner receives an incentive payment from a third-party platform or a share of the fees charged by the platform, it must be disclosed to the tenant/resident upfront.

chunks.heading_path: Secondary dwellings > Scenario 2 > Special terms
chunks.body:
The agreement should also include any special terms outlining arrangements for:
- access to the dwelling
- parking spaces
- mail management
- access to and use of clotheslines and rubbish bins
- internet charges
- pool and garden maintenance.

title: RTA: Social housing
licence: CC BY 3.0 AU, © The State of Queensland Residential Tenancies Authority

chunks.heading_path: Social housing
chunks.body:
New rental application forms are available for National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) specialist disability accommodation (SDA) for general tenancies and rooming accommodation. Read our news article for more information.
Social housing is an alternative to the private rental market for people who need housing. In Queensland, there are two types of social housing:
- public housing, which is managed by the Department of Housing and Public Works (the department)
- community housing, which is delivered by non-government organisations, local governments and community organisations.
Public and community housing tenancies are covered by the Residential Tenancies and Rooming Accommodation Act 2008 (the Act), but exemptions and additional rights apply.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Tenancy agreements
chunks.body:
Tenants renting directly from the department will have a State tenancy agreement with the Queensland Government. The agreement is a legal contract between the department and the tenant which outlines rights and obligations of both parties.
Community housing organisations will provide written general tenancy agreements or rooming accommodation agreements outlining rights and obligations.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Application Form
chunks.body: Property managers/owners must use a standardised tenancy application form ( Form 22 / R22) however, this does not apply to relevant lessors. Section 57B(7) of the Act defines relevant lessors.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Exemptions and additional rights
chunks.body: Certain sections of the Act have exemptions or additional rights if managed by a public or community housing provider. The main differences are outlined below.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Exemptions and additional rights > Rent increase exemptions
chunks.body:
If a community housing provider receives funding under the Housing Act 2003 or the Community Services Act 2007 and the rent payable is determined by household income, the provider has an exemption and is not required to:
- provide tenants with evidence of previous rent increases
- wait 12 months between rent increases.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Exemptions and additional rights > Requests to transfer a tenancy or sublet
chunks.body:
Tenants need to seek agreement in writing from their housing provider to transfer their tenancy to someone else or sublet the property if:
- they live in Queensland Government public housing
- they live in community housing, and their housing provider receives financial or other help from the Queensland Government to supply rented accommodation.
The provider is not required to be reasonable when considering the request.
The tenant may not apply to the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) for an order to change the housing provider’s decision.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Exemptions and additional rights > Notice to leave because of serious breach
chunks.body:
Public or community housing providers can give a tenant notice to leave due to a serious breach. The minimum notice period is 7 days.
The housing provider may give notice if they reasonably believe the tenant, an occupant, a guest of the tenant or a person allowed on the property by the tenant has:
- used the property or any property adjoining or adjacent to it for an illegal activity
- destroyed or seriously damaged a part of the property
- endangered another person in the property or nearby
- interfered significantly with the reasonable peace, comfort or privacy of another tenant.
A housing provider may form a reasonable belief that a property has been used for an illegal activity regardless of whether anyone has been convicted or found guilty of an offence.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Exemptions and additional rights > Applications to QCAT for a termination order
chunks.body:
Managing parties can make an urgent application to QCAT for a termination order due to:
- objectionable behaviour – if the tenant uses verbal abuse, harassment, intimidation, or causes serious nuisance or danger
- damage or injury – if the tenant has damaged the property or injured people.
However, in public and community housing, providers can also apply for termination for the above reasons if the behaviour, damage or injury was from an occupant, a guest of the tenant or a person allowed on the property by the tenant.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Exemptions and additional rights > Accommodation not covered by the Act
chunks.body: Some types of accommodation that may be provided by community housing providers are not covered by the Act, such as crisis and emergency accommodation, and the first 13 weeks of approved supported accommodation.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > Support from the RTA
chunks.body: Public and community housing tenants, residents and providers can access information on the RTA website and contact us for information, noting the exemptions above.

chunks.heading_path: Social housing > More information
chunks.body:
Visit the department’s page on Public and community housing, or contact your local Housing Service Centre.
If you are experiencing homelessness or are at risk of homelessness, call the Homeless Hotline on 1800 474 753.
